knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4

```

Many variables observed once a year depend on drought. Tree-ring widths,
crop yields, the annual flow of a river or the level of a reservoir at the
end of the summer are examples. Each of them responds to the water balance
of a particular part of the year, accumulated over a particular length of
time. A crop may depend on the rain of the three months before harvest. A
reservoir may integrate the water balance of a whole year.

The SPEI and the SPI can be computed at many time scales. The value of the
index in a given month at a time scale of `s` months summarizes the water
balance of the `s` months ending in that month. So the index at a month
and a time scale defines a window of time. Correlating the annual series
with the index in every month and at every time scale shows which window
the series responds to most. The function `scale_scan()` does this, and
`scale_extract()` gives the index series of the chosen window.

This approach has been used to relate the SPEI and the SPI to tree-ring
growth across a climatic gradient (Pasho et al., 2011), to map the time
scales at which vegetation responds to drought across the world's biomes
(Vicente-Serrano et al., 2013), and to study how thinning changes the
sensitivity of tree growth to hydric and thermal stress in four widely
planted pine species (Manrique-Alba et al., 2025).

## The data

The `tarazona` dataset has the growth of Aleppo pines (*Pinus halepensis*)
in a plantation at Tarazona, in the Ebro valley (Spain, 785 m a.s.l.), and
the climate of the site. The trees are in the control plot of a thinning
experiment, which was not thinned (Manrique-Alba et al., 2020). Growth is
measured as the basal area increment (BAI, in cm² per year) of 18 cores
from 11 trees, from 1959 to 2017. The climate comes from the gridded
dataset of the Spanish drought monitor (Vicente-Serrano et al., 2017), and
has 48 periods per year (four per month) from 1961 to 2020. See
`?Datasets` for the details.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(SPEI)

data(tarazona)
names(tarazona)
bai <- tarazona$bai
clim <- tarazona$clim
```

Most of this vignette uses monthly data. The precipitation and the
reference evapotranspiration (ETo) are totals per period, so the monthly
values are the sums of each group of four periods. The water balance is the
precipitation minus the ETo:

```{r}
to_monthly <- function(x) {
  ts(colSums(matrix(x, nrow = 4)), start = c(1961, 1), frequency = 12)
}
bal <- to_monthly(clim[, "PRCP"]) - to_monthly(clim[, "ETO"])
```

The original 48-period data are used at the end of this vignette (see
'Other frequencies') and in `vignette("weekly")`.

## The annual series

The annual series must contain only the signal that we want to relate to
drought. Other sources of variation over time should be removed first.
Crop yields usually grow over the years because of better varieties and
management. Tree-ring widths get narrower as the tree grows. The BAI of a
young tree grows with its size, and then levels off or declines. These
trends are not related to drought, but they add variance to the series,
and they can create spurious correlations with any index that also has a
trend.

The BAI of the cores shows these trends, and large differences in growth
rate between cores:

```{r, fig.alt = "Basal area increment of the 18 cores of the Tarazona control plot from 1959 to 2017. Growth rises during the first years of each core, and the cores differ in their level of growth."}
matplot(bai$year, bai[, -1],
  type = "l", lty = 1, col = "grey40",
  xlab = "Year", ylab = "BAI (cm2/year)"
)
```

In dendrochronology the trend is removed from each series before the
series are averaged. The cores start in different years, so removing the
trend after averaging would mix the trends of cores of different ages. Here
we log-transform each core and subtract a smoothing spline with four
degrees of freedom. The log makes the variance of the series more similar
between cores and over time, and the difference of logs is the log of the
ratio between the BAI and its trend. Each core becomes a series of
relative growth around zero:

```{r}
# log(BAI) minus a smoothing spline fitted to log(BAI), for one core
detrend_core <- function(x, year, df = 4) {
  ok <- !is.na(x)
  fit <- smooth.spline(year[ok], log(x[ok]), df = df)
  x[ok] <- log(x[ok]) - predict(fit, year[ok])$y
  x
}
rbai <- sapply(bai[, -1], detrend_core, year = bai$year)
rbai <- ts(rbai, start = bai$year[1], frequency = 1)
```

A flexible spline also removes part of the slow variation that is due to
climate, such as a dry decade. Stiffer curves keep more of it. Other
methods (e.g. negative exponential curves, or the ones in the `dplR`
package) can be used in the same way. Whatever the method, detrend the
series before calling `scale_scan()`. The argument `detrend = TRUE` only
removes a linear trend from the averaged series, which is enough for
simpler cases such as a crop yield that grows steadily over the years.

The average of the detrended cores in each year is the chronology of the
site:

```{r, fig.alt = "Mean of the detrended BAI of the 18 cores (the site chronology) from 1959 to 2017, fluctuating around zero with strong drops in some years"}
chron <- ts(rowMeans(rbai, na.rm = TRUE), start = bai$year[1])
plot(chron, xlab = "Year", ylab = "Detrended BAI (log ratio)")
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
depth <- rowSums(!is.na(bai[, -1]))
```

The number of cores per year is low at the start. Until
`r max(bai$year[depth == 1])` the chronology rests on a single core, and
from 1970 on it has `r min(depth[bai$year >= 1970])` cores or more. The
climate data start in 1961, so the first two years are not used.

The annual series is a time series with frequency 1, or a data frame with
the years in the first column and the values in the other columns.

## Running the scan

`scale_scan()` takes the water balance, computes the SPEI at the time
scales in `scales`, and correlates the annual series with the index in each
month and at each time scale. Here the annual series has one column per
core. All the values of each year are averaged (see 'Several annual
series'):

```{r}
sc <- scale_scan(bal, rbai, scales = 1:24)
sc
```

The best window is `r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]` at a time scale of
`r sc$best$scale[1]` months, i.e. the water balance from
`r month.name[(sc$best$cycle[1] - sc$best$scale[1]) %% 12 + 1]` to
`r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]`. Its correlation with the chronology is
r = `r round(sc$best$r[1], 2)` over `r sc$best$n[1]` years. There is no
significant negative window. Growth is larger in the years in which this
part of the year is wetter than usual.

Each window is defined by a month and a time scale. The SPEI of a month at
a time scale of `s` months summarizes the water balance accumulated over
the `s` months that end in that month. So the SPEI of
`r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]` at `r sc$best$scale[1]` months measures
whether the period from
`r month.name[(sc$best$cycle[1] - sc$best$scale[1]) %% 12 + 1]` to
`r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]` of each year was wetter or drier than
usual, and its value is known at the end of
`r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]`. For the tree, the result means that the
width of each ring depends on the water accumulated from the start of the
year to the end of the summer, which includes the soil water recharged in
winter and the water available during the growing season. In the same month,
shorter or longer windows correlate less: r =
`r round(sc$cor[sc$best$cycle[1], "1"], 2)` for that month alone (time
scale 1) and r = `r round(sc$cor[sc$best$cycle[1], "12"], 2)` for the
whole year to `r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]` (time scale 12).

For comparison, the average of the raw BAI with a linear trend removed
(`detrend = TRUE`) gives:

```{r}
sc_raw <- scale_scan(bal, ts(bai[, -1], start = bai$year[1]),
  scales = 1:24, detrend = TRUE
)
sc_raw$best[1, ]
```

The window is the same, with a slightly lower correlation
(r = `r round(sc_raw$best$r[1], 2)`). Here the simple approach gives
almost the same result, because most cores are mature and the year-to-year
variation is large. This will not hold in general, for example with young
trees or with cores of very different ages.

## Reading the heatmap

The `plot` method draws the correlations as a heatmap. The months are on
the horizontal axis and the time scales on the vertical axis. The dots
mark the cells that are significant after adjusting for multiple testing,
and the black outline shows the best window:

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the correlation between the Tarazona BAI chronology and the SPEI by month and time scale. The highest correlations are from June to September at time scales of about 6 to 12 months."}
plot(sc)
```

The correlations are highest from June to September, at time scales of
about 6 to 12 months. In other words, growth depends on the water balance
accumulated from the previous autumn or winter to the end of the summer.
With `sig = "mask"` the non-significant cells are left blank.

By default the colours are proportional to the squared correlation, with
its sign (`colour = "r2"`). This spreads the colours over the high
correlations, which are the ones of interest, while the legend still shows
the correlation. With `colour = "r"` the colours are proportional to the
correlation itself:

```{r, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "The same heatmap with colours proportional to the correlation instead of the squared correlation; the differences among the high correlations are less visible."}
plot(sc, colour = "r")
```

The results are kept in the object. `sc$cor` holds the correlations, with
one row per month and one column per time scale. `sc$p` and `sc$p.adj`
hold the p-values before and after the adjustment, and `sc$n` the number
of years used in each cell.

```{r}
round(sc$cor[6:9, c(1, 3, 6, 8, 12)], 2)
```

## The best windows and multiple testing

The best windows are the cells with the highest and the lowest
correlation, among those that are significant:

```{r}
sc$best
```

The scan above tests `r sum(!is.na(sc$cor))` cells. With so many tests,
some cells will have a low p-value by chance. At a 5% level, about 14 of
288 cells would be 'significant' with an annual series of pure noise. For
this reason the p-values are adjusted for multiple testing, across all the
cells. The default method, Holm's, keeps the probability of any false
positive among all the cells below `alpha`. Other methods can be chosen
with `p.adjust` (see `?p.adjust`).

To see the effect of the adjustment we scan a **synthetic** annual series
of pure noise, which has no relation to the climate:

```{r}
set.seed(1)
noise <- ts(rnorm(57), start = 1961)
sc_none <- scale_scan(bal, noise, scales = 1:24, p.adjust = "none")
sum(sc_none$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
sc_holm <- scale_scan(bal, noise, scales = 1:24)
sum(sc_holm$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
```

Without the adjustment `r sum(sc_none$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)`
cells are significant, and the best of them would be reported as the best
window. With the adjustment `r sum(sc_holm$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)`
are. The Tarazona
chronology has a strong signal, and many cells remain significant after
the adjustment
(`r sum(sc$p.adj <= 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)` of `r sum(!is.na(sc$cor))`).

The adjustment is conservative, because neighbouring cells share most of
their data. With short series it may leave no significant cell even when
there is a real signal. The unadjusted p-values are always in `sc$p`.

## Conditions of the previous year

Some annual series also depend on the conditions of the previous year. Tree
growth, for example, often depends on the water stored at the end of the
previous growing season. Time scales longer than the month reach into the
previous year (a time scale of 12 in March covers April of the previous
year to March), but they always include the months of the current year
too. The argument `lag` scans the months of previous years directly:
`lag = 0:1` correlates the annual series of year Y with the index of year
Y and of year Y-1.

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the correlation between the Tarazona BAI chronology and the SPEI, for the months of the previous and the current year. The correlations with the months of the previous year are weak; the highest ones are in the summer of the current year."}
sc_lag <- scale_scan(bal, rbai, scales = 1:24, lag = 0:1)
sc_lag$best
plot(sc_lag)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
prev <- sc_lag$rows$lag == 1
r_prev <- max(abs(sc_lag$cor[prev, ]), na.rm = TRUE)
p_prev <- min(sc_lag$p.adj[prev, ], na.rm = TRUE)
```

The rows are now in chronological order. `Jan-1` to `Dec-1` are the
months of the previous year, and `Jan` to `Dec` those of the current year.
The best window is the same as before, in the current year. In the months
of the previous year, the largest correlation (in absolute value) is
`r round(r_prev, 2)`, and no cell is significant (smallest adjusted
p-value `r signif(p_prev, 2)`). So at this site the water balance of the
previous year matters only through the long time scales of the current
year, which reach into it. The
`lag` column of `best` gives the year. The adjustment of the p-values
covers all the cells, so the scan with `lag = 0:1` is stricter than one
with `lag = 0`.

## Extracting the series of a window

`scale_extract()` returns the annual series of the index for a window, by
default the best positive one. It is aligned with the annual series: for a
window with a lag of one year, the value of year Y is the index of year
Y-1.

```{r}
spei_best <- scale_extract(sc)
window(spei_best, end = 1970)
```

The series covers all the years of the climate data (here 1961 to 2020),
so it does not span the same years as the annual series. Use
`ts.intersect()` to align them by year before using them together in other
models. Note that `lm()` does not align time series by itself.

```{r}
d <- ts.intersect(chron, spei_best)
fit <- lm(chron ~ spei_best, data = d)
summary(fit)$r.squared
```

Plotting the two series together shows how closely the index of the best
window follows the annual series. They are in different units, so here the
chronology is standardized (mean 0, standard deviation 1) to plot it on
the scale of the index:

```{r, fig.alt = "Time plot of the standardized Tarazona BAI chronology and the SPEI of the best window (August, 8-month scale) from 1961 to 2017. The two series follow each other, with the lowest values of both in the driest years."}
chron_std <- (chron - mean(chron)) / sd(chron)
spei_plot <- window(spei_best, end = 2017)
plot(spei_plot,
  type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(c(spei_plot, chron_std), na.rm = TRUE),
  xlab = "Year", ylab = "Standardized value"
)
lines(window(chron_std, start = 1961), col = "black", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 0, lty = 3)
legend("bottomleft", c("BAI chronology (standardized)", "SPEI, best window"),
  col = c("black", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n"
)
```

Any other window can be extracted by giving `cycle`, `scale` and `lag`:

```{r}
spei_jun3 <- scale_extract(sc, cycle = 6, scale = 3, lag = 0)
```

The correlation of the best window is chosen as the highest of many. It is
biased upwards, so the strength of the relationship should be checked with
independent data when possible.

## Options of the index

Options for `spei()` can be passed through `scale_scan()`, for example a
reference period or a kernel. With `index = "spi"` the SPI is computed
instead, from a precipitation series.

```{r}
prcp <- to_monthly(clim[, "PRCP"])
sc_spi <- scale_scan(prcp, rbai,
  scales = 1:24, index = "spi",
  distribution = "PearsonIII"
)
sc_spi$best
```

The SPI gives the same window, with a correlation of
`r round(sc_spi$best$r[1], 2)`. At this site the variation of the water
balance between years comes mostly from the precipitation.

The index can also be computed beforehand and passed with
`index = "precomputed"`, as a time series with one column per time scale.
The time scales are taken from the column names, or given in `scales`:

```{r}
idx <- sapply(c(1, 3, 6, 12), function(s) {
  spei(bal, s, verbose = FALSE)$fitted
})
idx <- ts(idx, start = c(1961, 1), frequency = 12)
colnames(idx) <- c("SPEI-1", "SPEI-3", "SPEI-6", "SPEI-12")
sc_pre <- scale_scan(idx, rbai, index = "precomputed")
sc_pre$best
```

With only these four time scales, the best window is
`r month.name[sc_pre$best$cycle[1]]` at `r sc_pre$best$scale[1]` months.

This is useful to scan an index computed elsewhere, or a set of time scales
computed once and used for several annual series.

## Other frequencies

The scan is not limited to monthly data. The position of each value in the
year comes from the frequency of the time series. Weekly data (frequency
52) give one row per week, labelled `W1` to `W52`. Other frequencies give
one row per period, labelled `P1`, `P2`, etc. The time scales are then in
periods.

The original analysis of these data used the 48 periods per year of the
Spanish drought monitor (Manrique-Alba et al., 2025). We scan time scales
from 4 to 96 periods (1 to 24 months) in steps of 4:

```{r}
bal48 <- clim[, "PRCP"] - clim[, "ETO"]
sc48 <- scale_scan(bal48, rbai, scales = seq(4, 96, by = 4))
sc48$best
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
p48 <- sc48$best$cycle[1]
s48 <- sc48$best$scale[1]
q48 <- c("first", "second", "third", "fourth")[(p48 - 1) %% 4 + 1]
```

The best window ends in period `r p48`, the `r q48` quarter of
`r month.name[ceiling(p48 / 4)]`, and has a time scale of `r s48` periods
(`r s48 / 4` months), with r = `r round(sc48$best$r[1], 2)`. The monthly
scan found a window of `r sc$best$scale[1]` months ending in
`r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]`. The heatmap shows that many neighbouring
cells have almost the same correlation, so the exact position and length
of the best window are not well determined. Manrique-Alba et al. (2025)
used period 34 and a time scale of 12 months for this site, with a
different model that included the thinned plots.

```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the correlation between the Tarazona BAI chronology and the SPEI computed with 48 periods per year, by period and time scale. The highest correlations are in late summer at time scales of about 30 to 50 periods."}
plot(sc48)
```

See `vignette("weekly")` for how to compute the indices with weekly and
other non-monthly data.

## Several annual series

Often there are several series for the same site, such as several trees, or
several fields of the same crop. There are two ways to analyse them.

The first one is to average them into a single series, and scan it once.
This is what we did above. `y` can be a time series with one column per
series, a data frame with the years in the first column and one column per
series, or a data frame with repeated years (one row per year and series).
All the values of each year are averaged. `y.count` keeps the number of
values in each year. The long format gives the same result as the matrix:

```{r}
long <- data.frame(
  year = rep(bai$year, ncol(rbai)),
  bai = as.vector(rbai)
)
head(long[!is.na(long$bai), ])
scale_scan(bal, long, scales = 1:24)$best[1, ]
```

The second one is to scan each series on its own:

```{r}
per_core <- lapply(colnames(rbai), function(core) {
  scale_scan(bal, rbai[, core], scales = 1:24)$best[1, ]
})
per_core <- do.call(rbind, per_core)
per_core$r <- round(per_core$r, 2)
per_core$p.adj <- signif(per_core$p.adj, 2)
cbind(core = colnames(rbai), per_core[, c("label", "scale", "r", "p.adj")])
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
same <- sum(per_core$label == sc$best$label[1])
```

Most cores (`r same` of `r nrow(per_core)`) have their best window in
`r month.name[sc$best$cycle[1]]`, but with time scales from `r min(per_core$scale)` to
`r max(per_core$scale)` months, and correlations from
`r min(per_core$r)` to `r max(per_core$r)`. The average has a stronger
signal than all but `r sum(per_core$r > round(sc$best$r[1], 2))` of the
single cores, because the individual noise cancels out. This is the standard way of building tree-ring chronologies.
But averaging is only valid if all the series share the same climate data
and respond to it in a similar way. It also hides any difference between
sites or individuals. If the series are on different scales, standardize
them before averaging. Here the detrending already puts all the cores on
the same scale.

Scanning each series gives a window for each one, so it can reveal
different responses, and each series can have its own climate data. But
each scan has more noise, and there are more tests in total.
